deploymentModel.description: Each distinct local port is assumed to become a distinct subdomain of one registrable domain (cross-origin, same-site).

findings.title: Cookies from localhost:8010 are also sent to 6 other servers on this machine
findings.summary:
Cookies have no concept of a port. RFC 6265 section 8.5 states it plainly: "cookies do not provide isolation by port". The Set-Cookie grammar has no port attribute, and the browser keys the jar by host alone. So every app you run on 127.0.0.1 shares one cookie jar, regardless of port.

Two consequences, and teams hit both. First, your app can read -- and silently overwrite -- another local app's session cookie, including one from an unrelated project. Second, this is the opposite of your production topology, where app.example.com and api.example.com are separate hosts that share cookies only if you set Domain deliberately. Neither sharing behaviour you see locally is the one you ship.

Right now this is not hypothetical: 127.0.0.1:3001, 127.0.0.1:5173, 127.0.0.1:5432, 127.0.0.1:8000, 127.0.0.1:8001, 127.0.0.1:9000 are listening and inside the same jar.

evidence.label: host-only cookies in the shared jar

fix: Do not rely on port separation for isolation. It does not exist.
Give each app a distinct hostname during development so the jars are genuinely separate.
If two local apps must not see each other's cookies, distinct hostnames are the only mechanism that works.

refs.title: RFC 6265 section 8.5 - Weak Confidentiality (cookies are not isolated by port)

findings.title: Session-shaped cookie "csrftoken" has no Secure attribute
findings.summary: It could not have one: a Secure cookie cannot be set over plain HTTP, so this is the expected local result. That is exactly the problem. Whatever sets Secure in production is a code path that did not run here, so this run says nothing about whether it works. Without Secure in production, the cookie is sent over any plain-HTTP request to the same host and can be read or overwritten by a network attacker.
findings.subject: csrftoken

evidence.label: Set-Cookie
evidence.value: csrftoken=A5MGNjl55DKXwj7xfprle3XoPs9lZGuk; expires=Thu, 02 Sep 2027 22:21:24 GMT; Max-Age=31449600; Path=/; SameSite=Lax

fix: Confirm the production configuration sets Secure, and prove it rather than assuming it.
Prefer terminating TLS locally over branching on the environment, so one code path serves both.

findings.title: "csrftoken" comes from Django, whose Secure flag is an environment setting (CSRF_COOKIE_SECURE)
findings.summary:
Django ships CSRF_COOKIE_SECURE = False by default. A CSRF cookie without Secure can be overwritten by a network attacker on a sibling HTTP origin.

The local run exercised the branch where that setting is off. Whether the production branch is configured correctly is not observable from here -- which is the point of flagging it.
findings.subject: csrftoken

evidence.label: observed
evidence.value: csrftoken=A5MGNjl55DKXwj7xfprle3XoPs9lZGuk; expires=Thu, 02 Sep 2027 22:21:24 GMT; Max-Age=31449600; Path=/; SameSite=Lax

fix: Verify CSRF_COOKIE_SECURE is enabled in the production configuration, and add a test that asserts it.
Better: serve HTTPS locally so the same configuration path runs in both places.

findings.title: An absolute URL points back at the app's own loopback origin
findings.summary:
Absolute URLs pointing back at the page's own origin. These are generated server-side rather than hardcoded, and they follow whatever host the app believes it is serving from. They only break if that base-URL setting is still a loopback address in production -- Laravel APP_URL and ASSET_URL, Django and Rails default_url_options, Next.js NEXT_PUBLIC_SITE_URL and NEXTAUTH_URL are the usual ones.

Found by scanning the bodies the dev server actually served during this run. That means two things: a value a production build would replace can still show up here, and a value in code that did not load will not show up at all. Check the quoted line before acting.
findings.subject: self-origin-absolute
fix: Check the base-URL setting for your framework and make sure the production value is the deployed origin, not a loopback address.
Laravel: APP_URL and ASSET_URL. Next.js: NEXT_PUBLIC_SITE_URL and NEXTAUTH_URL. Rails: default_url_options. Django: whatever feeds build_absolute_uri behind a proxy.
Where a relative URL would do, prefer it: it cannot be misconfigured.

findings.title: Requests went to 1 origin
findings.summary: How each origin is classified today, and how it is classified under the assumed deployment model. The model is printed at the top of the report and can be changed with --domain and --map.

refs.title: Fetch Standard - CORS protocol and credentials

limitations: This predicts behaviour on a real HTTPS origin. It does not prove it. The only proof is serving the app from that origin.
It observes only code paths that actually executed during the run. Coverage of findings equals coverage of the run, which is why --flow matters more than any individual rule.
Chrome family only (Chrome, Chromium, Edge). Firefox and Safari differ on SameSite defaults, cookie partitioning and secure-context edge cases.
A clean result means "no findings in what was exercised". It never means "safe".
The deployment model is an assumption, printed above. Change it with --domain, --map and --cross-site if it does not match your topology.
Source scanning reads what the dev server served. A production build may substitute different values, and code that did not load was not scanned.
Findings from a single page load do not cover other routes. Run the analyzer against the routes that matter.
